details:
Red Route, developed by Team Peixonautas, explores how planetary data and immersive interfaces can help future astronauts understand their surroundings, plan traversable routes, and make informed decisions on Mars.

Our presentation identifies several challenges that motivate this concept: radiation exposure, potentially hazardous soil and fine dust, difficult terrain, extreme temperatures, and the thin Martian atmosphere. Unplanned travel could increase exposure to these hazards and complicate resource management and the return journey.

Our proposed solution is an augmented-reality interface integrated into an astronaut’s helmet. It would bring navigation, scientific information, and mission-support tools directly into the explorer’s field of view. To demonstrate aspects of this concept, we developed a browser-based prototype with three complementary experiences: an interactive 2D map, a 3D terrain viewer, and a mobile first-person visualization inspired by a helmet display.

The implemented route planner uses an A* search algorithm to suggest paths between selected starting and destination points. Users can adjust the importance of horizontal distance, terrain slope, elevation gain, and manually interpreted terrain conditions. Blocked areas prevent passage, while difficult areas increase route cost. Users can also decide how unknown terrain should affect planning.

Optional environmental criteria accept imported numerical grids or explicitly labeled synthetic scenarios. Radiation costs depend on estimated exposure during travel at a configurable constant speed. Temperature costs depend on departure from a selected temperature range. Magnetic-field costs are experimental preferences based on field magnitude and do not imply protection against radiation. The prototype does not automatically retrieve live environmental maps.

Gale Crater is our main demonstration area. The local planner uses a 30-meter HRSC digital terrain model covering approximately 13 by 12 kilometers near Curiosity and the foothills of Mount Sharp. A local terrain service can retrieve additional elevation coverage for other regions and larger distances, reporting the resolution selected. Routes can be exported as GeoJSON with their parameters, calculated metrics, and source information.

The 3D and mobile first-person experiences help users understand the landscape spatially. The mobile experience includes device-orientation controls, terrain-following movement, route visualization, and floating map panels. Its Gale terrain uses prepared HiRISE-derived elevation data alongside broader MOLA/HRSC coverage.

Our presentation illustrates potential applications in mineral-resource exploration, access to difficult regions, and habitat or survival-system studies. Locations such as Bradbury Landing, Yellowknife Bay, the Bagnold Dunes, Mount Sharp, and Gediz Vallis provide context for these scenarios. They are illustrative mission examples rather than validated expedition routes.

The broader Red Route concept includes oxygen and energy budgeting, return-trip feasibility assessment, walking or rover recommendations, hazard warnings, emergency location sharing, and astronaut and rover tracking. These remain proposed extensions rather than established capabilities of the current prototype.

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet, Three.js, Node.js, Vite, GeoTIFF.js, and Python preparation scripts. Route calculations run in a Web Worker to keep the interface responsive.

Red Route’s creative contribution is the combination of adjustable route planning, scientific terrain data, and immersive visualization within a mission-support concept. We considered planetary coordinates, physical terrain scale, missing data, source resolution, uncertain terrain, and reproducibility. Our intended impact is to support better-planned exploration, more informed resource use, and clearer identification of potential risks. The current system is an educational and research prototype, not an operationally validated astronaut navigation system.
